title: Rationalism and Divergent Sinomodernity
gist: Argues that American AI forecasters, steeped in Bay Area rationalism, wrongly expect China to nationalize or restrict open-weight AI; China instead keeps an open-weight, diffusion-focused, state-supervised strategy while Chinese labs run on roughly one-tenth the capex and far lower valuations. The key implication is sustained price compression against US frontier labs, with timing of any Chinese policy shift a critical variable.

insights.claim: Xi Jinping's July 2026 WAIC speech, the day after Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, reaffirmed China's open-source stance, undercutting the Western expectation that China would have to abandon open weights as frontier costs rise.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Open-weight Chinese supply of near-frontier models should be underwritten as durable, not as a transient.
insights.quote: “We should adhere to the principle of openness,”
insights.locator: Moonshot AI, one of China’s largest

insights.claim: A widespread Western 'Mythos moment' theory holds that China will abruptly restrict open-weight AI once models become dangerous; the author argues the Chinese state keeps defying this prediction.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Positioning that assumes an imminent Chinese clampdown on open models (restoring US lab pricing power) is exposed to timing risk.
insights.locator: For many in the English-speaking world

insights.claim: Chinese AI policy documents frame AI as diffusion, standards-setting and economic value-add; the AI+ Plan does not mention competition or America, in contrast with the US winner-take-all LLM-scaling race framing.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: China is optimising for broad application-layer diffusion rather than a superintelligence race, which favors cheap, widely distributed models.
insights.locator: This does not seem to be how the Chinese see it.

insights.claim: China retains strong regulatory levers over models (pre-deployment registration and review via provincial and central CAC, ability to force model changes), which helps explain why it can tolerate wide access to capable open-weight models.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Control over deployment rather than release lowers the Chinese state's need to restrict open weights, so a policy reversal is less likely near term.
insights.locator: Today, the Chinese state retains a multitude of regulatory tools

insights.claim: Chinese state support (billions in compute vouchers, support for small firms, regional labs) sustains many labs releasing open-weight models built partly via distillation from American frontier models, with a shifting substrate of application-specialist firms below.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: The Chinese AI stack is a decentralized, subsidized ecosystem; value capture sits in application specialization.
insights.locator: Encouraged by billions of dollars worth of compute vouchers

themes.theme: Open-weight price compression vs US labs

insights.claim: Continued availability of highly capable Chinese open-weight models erodes the moat, profits and expected value of American frontier labs, which is what underpins their capital access and that of the whole AI infrastructure chain (cloud, neoclouds).
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: The AI buildout financing thesis depends on frontier pricing power; open-weight commoditization is a core risk to infrastructure capex returns.
insights.locator: The most immediate implication of the continued availability

insights.claim: Industry analyst reporting cited by the author says Anthropic's inference margins rose from 38% to 70% as revenue grew, suggesting frontier complex inference remains highly profitable even as lower-complexity usage may be ceded to cheap competitors.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Watch Anthropic and OpenAI IPO disclosures for inference margin trajectory as the test of commoditization.
insights.locator: Industry analyst reporting from earlier this year

insights.claim: Anthropic is preparing a public offering later in 2026 and OpenAI is set to follow in 2027, which will turn inference margin and capital allocation from leaks into public disclosure.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: IPO filings become the key price-discovery event for whether frontier margins hold under Chinese price pressure.
insights.locator: As Anthropic prepares its public offering

insights.claim: A plausible scenario is that machine intelligence becomes 'too cheap to meter' for most usage, with enormous profits only at the frontier edge, a possibility the author says becomes less hypothetical daily.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Own the edge-of-capability and distribution layers rather than generic inference if commoditization continues.
insights.quote: There is a plausible world where machine intelligence becomes too cheap to meter for most usage
insights.locator: There is a plausible world

insights.claim: OpenAI cut token costs for GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% and Terra by 20%, which the author reads as an early sign of price pressure forcing US labs to cut costs.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Falling list prices at the leader suggest competitive pricing pressure is already hitting US lab revenue per token.
insights.locator: OpenAI has already cut token costs

insights.claim: Timing matters asymmetrically: if China reversed course on open weights within two months, value would flow back to US labs with little damage, but a year or more of price compression would be far more damaging.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: The risk to US lab valuations is duration of the open-weight regime, so forecasts of Chinese policy timing are a pricing variable.
insights.locator: If the Chinese government eventually moves away

insights.claim: The author cites Dean Ball (OpenAI) saying open-weight is decelerationist, and agrees this is plausible for the AI buildout narrowly, since price competition lowers the value frontier models accrue.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Even US insiders concede open weights are a headwind for buildout economics.
insights.locator: Dean Ball, Head of Strategic Futures

themes.theme: Chinese labs: monetizing while staying cheap

insights.claim: Chinese labs are monetizing while staying open: Moonshot's Kimi K3 license requires renegotiated commercial terms for non-Moonshot API users above $20 million annual revenue and branding display for businesses with over 100 million monthly users or meeting that revenue test.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Open-weight no longer means free; Chinese labs are building commercial moats via licensing, signaling expected policy stability.
insights.locator: Chinese labs seem to be actively working to monetize

insights.claim: DeepSeek lowered V4 costs by 75% earlier in 2026 but now seems likely to raise API prices substantially.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Chinese price floors may rise, a partial offset to the commoditization risk for US labs.
insights.locator: Further, after lowering V4 costs

insights.claim: In a leaked May 20 investor call, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng said prices are set to earn only reasonable profit, predicted DeepSeek frontier models would stay open-weight, and argued that those who take more will be beaten by those who take less.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Stated Chinese strategy is margin sacrifice for share, which directly challenges the high-margin US frontier model of value capture.
insights.quote: “Those who take more will be beaten by those who take less.”
insights.locator: The most candid view from a Chinese lab

insights.claim: The leaked Liang call was disclosed in July and disrupted DeepSeek's second fundraising round of the year.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Disclosure risk can briefly disrupt Chinese lab financing but the stated strategy is now public.
insights.locator: The May 20th call was leaked in July

insights.claim: Chinese firms are set to spend about one-tenth of what American firms spend on the AI buildout, yet raise at far lower valuations: DeepSeek raised $7.4 billion at $50 billion and began another raise at $74 billion, Alibaba is issuing $10 billion in equity for AI, versus Anthropic and OpenAI each valued near a trillion dollars.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Chinese labs need far lower returns and capex to compete, so a capital-intensity gap favors them in a price war; DeepSeek has a possible 2027 Shanghai IPO.
insights.locator: The Chinese labs seem to need a much lower profit

insights.claim: The 'AI 2027' scenario predicted that China's General Secretary would nationalize frontier AI research by mid-2026; that has not happened, and its authors concede 'China Wakes Up' has not occurred.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Forecasts built on Chinese convergence should be discounted; a track-record miss on the key geopolitical assumption.
insights.quote: “China Wakes Up” has not yet happened.
insights.locator: According to the scenario

insights.claim: American AI forecasts err because Bay Area rationalism assumes different polities share similar utility functions for the same technology once it reaches scale, deemphasizing contingent details like governing dynamics and culture.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: US AI-policy and AI-race narratives that rest on mirror-imaging China are likely mispriced.
insights.locator: There is a particular aspect of rationalist thinking

insights.claim: Rationalist framing is overrepresented at major AI labs and their social circles and is spreading to mainstream discourse, including p(doom)-style probabilities, often without people knowing its origin.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: US lab and policy narratives are shaped by a narrow intellectual subculture; discount accordingly.
insights.locator: Bay Area rationalism spread across an influential group of blogs

insights.claim: Using Yuk Hui's framework, deep learning is a shared technical 'tendency' while concerns like existential risk, labor displacement and cyberattacks are contingent 'facts'; rationalist forecasts overestimate tendencies and underestimate facts.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Forecast divergence between US and China should be sought in societal specifics, not in the technology.
insights.locator: In Cybernetics for the 21st Century

insights.claim: The author repeats a historical analogy: US assumption that economic liberalization would bring political liberalization in China led to deindustrialization and supply-chain dependencies still used as leverage, and misreading China on AI would be costlier and more irreversible.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Strategy built on mirror-imaging China carries repeated, compounding costs.
insights.locator: One of America’s greatest strategic mistakes

themes.theme: Labor structure drives divergent AI governance

insights.claim: If AI-driven job displacement drives government response, American office and professional workers face automation before Chinese manual workers, because digital intelligence arrives before physical robots (Kai-Fu Lee's 'Moravec's revenge').
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: US political pressure to regulate or slow AI is likely to build first; China faces less near-term labor-shock pressure.
insights.quote: “it’s far easier to build AI algorithms than to build intelligent robots.”
insights.locator: In his 2018 book AI Superpowers

insights.claim: Workforce structure data: 23% of Chinese workers were in primary agriculture and 29% in manufacturing and industry as of 2023, versus 43% of US workers in management and professional jobs, 18% in sales and office and 16% in services as of 2025.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: US white-collar exposure (about 77% in professional, office and service roles) makes it the first economy facing AI labor-market political pressure.
insights.locator: As of 2023, 23% of Chinese workers

insights.claim: China's security minister Chen Yixin's September 12 article on AI risks covered disinformation, cyberattacks, data leaks and military uses, and criticized 'monopoly' via technology controls and closed-source ecosystems, but did not mention job loss or safety concerns dominating US debate.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Chinese official risk framing targets US export controls and closed-source lead, consistent with continued open-weight strategy.
insights.locator: That same day, September 12th

insights.claim: In mid-September 2026 the US saw Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon's resignation over catastrophic risk and the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and xAI each endorsing pacing the frontier, while China's focus stayed on practical applications.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: US lab leadership is publicly endorsing slowdown, a regulatory and supply risk absent on the Chinese side.
insights.locator: Mid-September 2026 was a clear moment

insights.claim: China may be uninterested in pacing the frontier because US chip export controls already force it to pace, and the existing cybersecurity state lets the CAC order model changes unilaterally, removing the need for independent evaluators.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Export controls may reduce Chinese urgency about frontier racing, with hypotheses unproven.
insights.locator: Perhaps they are uninterested in pacing the frontier

insights.claim: The author warns that a Chinese policy shift could still occur as models self-improve, but argues timing (two months versus two years) and the nature of China's reaction are uncertain and need not mirror America's.
insights.speaker: Farrell Gregory
insights.so_what: Treat Chinese regime change in AI policy as a tail risk with unknown timing and direction.
insights.locator: It could be that this is just a matter of distinguishing between timelines
